lead: Things I’ve built, mostly with friends and mostly in a hurry. Each entry says what the thing does and which part was mine.

projects.name: Morro

figure.alt: Four maps comparing the change in precipitation under four simulated cloud-seeding methods
figure.caption: Precipitation change 126 hours after seeding, for four methods, over a Middle East drought.

paras: Morro is a simulator for the people who would have to decide on a weather intervention before a disaster arrives. It forecasts ten days ahead with two AI weather models, GraphCast and NVIDIA Earth2Studio, flags droughts and forming cyclones, then replays the forecast under each of four cloud-seeding methods and ranks them by how much they help.

I built the perturbation pipeline. Each seeding method becomes a physics-calibrated change to the model’s starting atmosphere, which then carries through the full ten-day rollout. I also trained the Random Forest classifiers that detect drought severity and cyclone formation from ERA5 reanalysis data. Built with Tej Kosaraju and Kieran P.
projects.note: A weekend simulation. A change in a forecast is not evidence that seeding would work in the real atmosphere.

projects.name: OceanOps

figure.alt: OceanOps mission control, with plume controls, a heat map off the California coast and modeled ocean chemistry
figure.caption: Mission control. The public demo runs on bundled ocean conditions.

paras: OceanOps is a shipboard planning tool for ocean alkalinity enhancement, a way of removing carbon by making seawater slightly less acidic. Change a vessel’s speed, discharge rate or feedstock and see how the modeled plume and the water chemistry respond, then plan fleet routes around marine traffic and protected areas.

My part was fleet telemetry over NATS with an HTTP fallback, the AI analysis panel, the map overlays, the simulation flow, and fixes to route rendering. Built with Akshat Choudhari and Yashmit Bhaverisetti.
projects.note: A planning prototype. The demo’s chemistry thresholds, plume and carbon estimates are illustrative.

projects.name: CourseLens
projects.meta: Data Science Teaching and Learning Lab · paper at SIGCSE TS 2027

figure.title: The Edit Is Not the End
figure.subtitle: CourseLens for Reviewing AI-Proposed Course Updates
figure.authors: Andrew Yang, Susana Haing, Thaarak Sriram, Chengyun Xu, Zhiqing Wang, Sam Lau
figure.caption: The paper CourseLens accompanies.

paras: Instructors have started asking AI coding agents to update whole courses: a new library version, a new dataset, a changed syllabus. The agent edits dozens of files, and someone has to check them before students see them. CourseLens lays the proposed edits out in the order the course is taught, shows each one in the rendered lecture or assignment, and uses the agent’s activity log to mark which files it changed, which it only checked, and which it never opened.
I’m one of the paper’s six authors and part of the team that built the tool, with Andrew Yang, Susana Haing, Chengyun Xu, Zhiqing Wang and Sam Lau.
projects.note: CourseLens never edits course files and doesn’t judge whether a change is correct. The instructor does.

projects.name: Triton Hub
projects.meta: A student dashboard for UC San Diego

figure.alt: Triton Hub dashboard showing sample coursework, email and deadlines
figure.caption: The public demo uses fictional courses and messages.

paras: Deadlines at UC San Diego arrive in several places at once. Triton Hub pulls Canvas assignments, grades and announcements, academic email and a personal calendar into one feed.

I wired live Canvas data into the assignment and announcement views, and built calendar events and completion tracking on Supabase. Built with Rayirth Dinesh, Siddharth Maddikayala and shrivassudharsan1.

projects.name: Solar Registry Screening

head: Rank
Example plant
Capacity
Score
figure.caption: Output of the bundled demo: five fictional installations go in, three qualify, each scored out of 100 by eleven rules.

paras: A public registry lists thousands of solar installations. This pipeline validates the records, filters them down to the ones that qualify, and ranks what is left with explicit rules, so every score comes with the points and reasons behind it.

The design rule is cheapest first. The deterministic ranking runs offline on registry fields alone, and only the shortlist goes on to geospatial matching or optional model-assisted scoring. Ambiguous matches are left unresolved.
projects.note: The public repository contains synthetic examples only. The scores illustrate a screening method, not investment advice.

projects.name: Arnold

figure.alt: Arnold showing a meal draft with portions and nutrition estimates, ready for review
figure.caption: A meal entry waits for review before it is saved.

paras: Arnold is a fitness journal you talk to. Describe a meal or a workout in plain English, check what Arnold understood, and only then save it.

I added plain-English meal and workout logging, USDA food lookup, exercise search and the voice flow to our hackathon prototype. For the public version I rebuilt logging so it previews portions and nutrients before anything is saved. The original was built with Shrish Premkrishna, Kenny and Jello.

projects.name: Wendy

figure.alt: Wendy’s planning chat with prompts for venue search, inquiry drafts and guest RSVPs
figure.caption: The demo uses fictional venues and never sends anything.

paras: Wendy keeps venue search, guest lists and planning conversations in one place. Set a budget and a guest count, shortlist venues, and it drafts an inquiry from details already in the conversation.

I built the venue-search tool, connected it to chat, and wrote the reservation-request flow that collects event details and drafts the inquiry. Built with Shrish Premkrishna, Aryaman Gandhi and Kenny.
